DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract
Larkspur Home, Operations, June 2026

1. Purpose
Our contract with our current standard-delivery carrier ends on 30 September 2026. This paper compares three shortlisted carriers and recommends which should carry our standard (two-to-four-day) parcels from October.

2. Volumes and requirements
We dispatch an average of 42,000 standard parcels a month: about 70% weigh under 2 kg (cushions, textiles, small homeware) and 30% weigh 2 to 10 kg (lamps, mirrors, small furniture). Our requirements are on-time delivery of at least 95%, a damage rate below 0.5%, full tracking, and a returns service.

Damage and loss matter to us commercially. Each damaged or lost parcel costs us on average £48 in replacement stock, return shipping and customer service time, and damaged items are the most common cause of one-star reviews.

3. Trial
Between 1 April and 31 May 2026, each shortlisted carrier delivered a share of our orders, allocated at random by the warehouse management system, about 5,000 parcels per carrier. We measured on-time delivery against the promised date, damage reported by customers within 14 days, and lost parcels.

Table 1. Prices and trial performance
Carrier | Price, under 2 kg | Price, 2-10 kg | On-time delivery | Damage rate | Lost per 10,000 parcels
SwiftDrop | £3.10 | £4.60 | 96.2% | 0.4% | 3
ParcelLine | £2.85 | £4.95 | 93.1% | 0.9% | 8
Meridian | £3.30 | £4.40 | 97.5% | 0.3% | 2

On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial, and all three offer full tracking and a returns service.

4. Cost comparison
Applying our 70/30 weight mix, the average cost per parcel is £3.55 for SwiftDrop, £3.48 for ParcelLine and £3.63 for Meridian. On 42,000 parcels a month, the monthly cost would be £149,100 for SwiftDrop, £146,160 for ParcelLine and £152,460 for Meridian. ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop and £6,300 a month against Meridian, or between about £35,000 and £76,000 a year.

5. Customer contact
"Where is my order?" contacts are our largest single category of customer service enquiry. During the trial, ParcelLine deliveries generated 6 such contacts per 1,000 parcels, compared with 11 for SwiftDrop and 10 for Meridian. ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts, and at an average handling cost of £3.20 per contact this would save about £670 a month at our volumes. From 1 May, ParcelLine parcels also carried our new proactive delivery-day text message, which we were testing on one carrier before rolling it out.

6. Other considerations
All three carriers can collect from our warehouse daily at 6 pm. ParcelLine and SwiftDrop offer a 12-month contract; Meridian requires 24 months. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled our peak-season volumes for other retailers of similar size, while ParcelLine's references were mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.

All three carriers integrate with our warehouse management system through standard interfaces, and none would require changes to our packing process or labelling. Each offers recipients a delivery-preference service to nominate a safe place or a neighbour, and each provides proof-of-delivery photographs, which our customer service team has found useful in resolving disputes.

7. Recommendation
ParcelLine offers the lowest delivery cost, met our service requirements in the trial and reduces customer contacts through its tracking app. We recommend awarding the standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from 1 October 2026, saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial" -- Table 1 shows ParcelLine's on-time delivery was 93.1%, below the 95% requirement. The claim (and the recommendation that ParcelLine 'met our service requirements') misreads the table; ParcelLine's 0.9% damage rate also fails the stated 0.5% requirement.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" -- The document states that from 1 May ParcelLine parcels alone also carried the new proactive delivery-day text message. That concurrent intervention confounds the comparison, so the lower contact rate cannot be attributed to ParcelLine's tracking app.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop" -- The cost comparison ignores the stated £48 cost of each damaged or lost parcel. ParcelLine's damage and loss rates (0.9% and 8 per 10,000) versus SwiftDrop's (0.4% and 3 per 10,000) imply about 231 extra problem parcels a month (about £11,100), far exceeding the £2,940 price saving; ParcelLine is likely the most expensive option overall.

REVIEW:
# Review: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract Comparison (Larkspur Home)

The trial is well designed, and the price arithmetic is correct. But the recommendation rests on a misreading of the trial results. **ParcelLine failed two of the four stated requirements.** Once damage and loss are costed, using the £48 figure the paper itself gives, ParcelLine becomes **the most expensive option**, not the cheapest.

## 1. ParcelLine failed the service requirements

Section 2 sets the requirements, and Table 1 shows how each carrier performed against them:

| Requirement | SwiftDrop | ParcelLine | Meridian |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-time delivery ≥ 95% | 96.2% ✅ | **93.1% ❌** | 97.5% ✅ |
| Damage rate < 0.5% | 0.4% ✅ | **0.9% ❌** | 0.3% ✅ |

The paper states that "on-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers," and the recommendation says ParcelLine "met our service requirements." Both statements contradict Table 1. ParcelLine's damage rate is more than twice the threshold, and two to three times that of the other carriers. It also lost the most parcels.

## 2. With damage and loss costed, ParcelLine is the most expensive

The price figures are correct. At the 70/30 weight mix, the cost per parcel is £3.55, £3.48 and £3.63, which gives £149,100, £146,160 and £152,460 a month. But section 2 itself says each damaged or lost parcel costs **£48**, and section 4 never uses that figure.

Monthly totals at 42,000 parcels:

| | SwiftDrop | ParcelLine | Meridian |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delivery price | £149,100 | £146,160 | £152,460 |
| Damaged parcels | 168 | 378 | 126 |
| Lost parcels | 12.6 | 33.6 | 8.4 |
| Damage and loss cost at £48 | £8,669 | £19,757 | £6,451 |
| "Where is my order?" contacts at £3.20 (11 / 6 / 10 per 1,000) | £1,478 | £806 | £1,344 |
| **Total monthly cost** | **£159,247** | **£166,723** | **£160,255** |
| Compared with the cheapest | — | **+£7,476** | +£1,008 |

On a total-cost basis, **ParcelLine costs about £90,000 a year more than SwiftDrop and about £78,000 more than Meridian**. That's even after giving it full credit for its lower contact rate. The headline "saving up to £76,000 a year" reverses the actual result. The cost above also excludes the reputational cost of more one-star reviews, which the paper itself links to damage.

## 3. The contact reduction can't be credited to the tracking app

From 1 May, which is half the trial, **only ParcelLine parcels carried the new proactive delivery-day text**. That text is designed to reduce "where is my order?" contacts. So the lower contact rate may come from the text, the app, or both, and the trial can't separate them.

The paper's conclusion that "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" isn't supported. If the text message produced the drop, rolling it out to whichever carrier wins should cut their contact rates too, and ParcelLine's advantage disappears. In any case the saving is small, about £540–£670 a month, against £6,000–£11,000 a month of extra damage cost.

The confound also undermines the trial's fairness: parcels were randomised between carriers, but the treatment wasn't the same for all of them. If the April-only figures are available, comparing them would give a cleaner result.

## 4. Lost-parcel figures rest on very small numbers

With about 5,000 parcels per carrier, rates of 2, 3 and 8 per 10,000 correspond to roughly **1, 1.5 and 4 actual parcels**. These are too few to rank the carriers reliably. The damage and on-time differences rest on larger numbers: about 15–45 damaged parcels per carrier, and roughly 150–350 late deliveries. Those differences are reasonably robust.

## 5. Peak-season risk

- The trial ran in April and May, a quiet period. The contract starts on 1 October, right before peak season.
- SwiftDrop and Meridian have handled peak volumes for retailers of similar size. ParcelLine's references are mainly fashion retailers with lighter parcels. Larkspur's 30% of heavier items (lamps, mirrors, small furniture) is exactly where damage is most likely.
- ParcelLine's trial performance is already the weakest, so it is the riskiest carrier for peak season.

## 6. Contract term

The 12-month term is described as a reason to choose ParcelLine, but **SwiftDrop also offers 12 months**, so it isn't a point of difference. The real trade-off is between SwiftDrop's 12-month term and Meridian's 24 months with slightly better performance.

## What holds up

- The trial design: live, randomised allocation, measured against clearly defined requirements.
- All the price arithmetic: the weighted averages, monthly costs and the £35,280 and £75,600 annual price differences.
- The £48 cost per damaged or lost parcel. It just needs to be used.
- Section 6's checks on collection times, system integration, delivery preferences and proof-of-delivery photos.

## What the evidence actually supports

**SwiftDrop** appears to be the strongest choice:

- it meets all four requirements
- it has the lowest total cost
- it has peak-season experience
- it offers the same 12-month flexibility

**Meridian** is a close second, with the best service figures at about £12,000 a year more, though it requires a 24-month commitment. If damage reduction is a priority, the board might weigh that against the longer term. **ParcelLine** shouldn't be recommended on this evidence.

## Suggested changes

1. Correct the on-time statement, and report ParcelLine's failures on both the on-time and damage thresholds.
2. Rebuild the cost comparison on a total-cost basis that includes damage, loss and customer contacts.
3. Remove the claim that the tracking app caused the drop in contacts. Report the effect of the text message separately, using April data if possible.
4. Add a caveat on the small lost-parcel numbers, and a section on peak-season risk.
5. Revise the recommendation in light of the above. On the evidence presented, that probably means SwiftDrop.
